claims.text: Introducing a selected dopant into a transition-metal catalyst will downshift the d-band center of the active metal sites.
Dopant atoms donate or withdraw electron density and thereby alter the local electronic environment of active sites.
The dopant-induced electronic change modulates adsorption and desorption strengths for reactants or reaction intermediates.
A downward-shifted d-band center stabilizes key adsorbates.
The dopant-induced electronic change improves catalytic turnover frequency.
The dopant-induced electronic change improves selectivity for the target product.
The dopant-induced electronic change improves catalyst durability.
Doping can retard deactivation by promoting removal of poisoning intermediates.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy binding-energy shifts can be used to infer a shift in the active metal's d-band center.
Moderate dopant loadings will produce stepwise improvements in turnover frequency.
Moderate dopant loadings will produce stepwise improvements in target-product selectivity.
Moderate dopant loadings will produce stepwise improvements in resistance to deactivation.
Excessive doping may reduce catalytic performance.
The performance loss at excessive dopant loading is caused by structural distortion.
The beneficial effect should hold only at moderate dopant concentrations and within 300–600 °C.
Very high dopant loading or substantially different reaction conditions may diminish the beneficial electronic and structural changes.
Dopant-induced lattice strain or particle agglomeration can mask or negate the proposed electronic effect and performance enhancement.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis broadly says that increasing dopant concentration will improve performance, whereas the predicted outcome and boundary specify a non-monotonic response in which only moderate loading is beneficial and excessive loading may reduce performance.
